name: Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis)
secondary_queries: how long does frozen shoulder last
seo_title: Frozen Shoulder Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Frozen shoulder pain and stiffness? Physical therapy in North Palm Beach paced to your stage, one-on-one since 1991. Medicare accepted. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Frozen shoulder slowly steals motion and sleep, and physical therapy paced to how irritable your shoulder is can ease pain while you work to win back your reach.
what_it_is: Your shoulder joint is wrapped in a strong sleeve of connective tissue called the capsule. In frozen shoulder, this capsule thickens, tightens and forms bands of scar-like tissue, so there is less room for the joint to move. The hallmark, according to the JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline, is a gradual loss of motion both when you lift the arm yourself and when someone else tries to move it, especially overhead and in rotation.

According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, frozen shoulder most often affects people between 40 and 60 and is more common in women. The JOSPT guideline reports that it affects 2% to 5.3% of the general population, with higher rates among people with diabetes or thyroid disease. A period of immobility after an injury, surgery or stroke also raises the risk.
symptoms: Dull or aching pain over the outer shoulder
Pain that is often worse at night and disturbs sleep
Pain that is strongest early on and when you move the arm
Stiffness that builds gradually over weeks to months
Trouble reaching overhead or rotating the arm
The same stiffness when someone else tries to move your arm for you
causes: Keeping the shoulder still after an injury, fracture, surgery or stroke
A previous frozen shoulder on the other side

how_therapy_helps.intro: Therapy aims to ease pain and recover motion without overloading an irritable joint. The JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline recommends stretching exercises with intensity matched to how irritable the shoulder is, and education about the natural course of the condition and how to modify activity. It also supports joint mobilization to reduce pain and improve motion. The same guideline notes stronger short-term relief when a physician's corticosteroid injection is combined with mobility and stretching exercises.
methods: Gentle, frequent stretches are used when the shoulder is very painful, and firmer, longer holds are added as it settles, following the JOSPT guideline's approach.
Hands-on mobilization directed at the shoulder joint can reduce pain and help increase motion, as the guideline describes.
Understanding how frozen shoulder typically progresses helps you set expectations and adjust activities so you keep using the arm without flaring it.
Guided movements help you use the motion you already have in daily tasks such as dressing and reaching.
Shoulder and shoulder blade strengthening is added as range improves, and the NHS lists strength work as part of physiotherapy for frozen shoulder.

first_visit: Your therapist measures shoulder motion in each direction, both when you move the arm and when it is moved for you, and compares it with your other side. You discuss how pain behaves at rest and at night and how quickly it settles after activity, which helps judge irritability. Your health history, including diabetes or thyroid conditions, and your hardest daily tasks guide the starting plan.
recovery: Frozen shoulder is slow. Mayo Clinic says overall recovery typically takes 1 to 3 years, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that full recovery may take up to 3 years, with most people improving without surgery. The NHS describes physiotherapy lasting at least 6 weeks. The JOSPT guideline reports that mild to moderate pain and stiffness may persist at 12 to 18 months, though many people report little or no disability by then. Your therapy plan changes as your shoulder moves through each phase.
self_care: Keep moving the shoulder gently every day instead of resting it completely.
Do the exercises a professional has given you, and avoid building your own strenuous routine.
Try a heat pack wrapped in a towel on the shoulder for up to 20 minutes.
Avoid forcing stretches into sharp pain, which can flare an irritable shoulder.
see_a_doctor: Seek emergency help right away for shoulder pain together with chest tightness, sweating or difficulty breathing (possible heart attack).
A shoulder that looks deformed, or intense pain with sudden swelling after a fall, needs urgent care.
A shoulder that turns red, warm and swollen needs a physician's evaluation.
Pain and stiffness that keep getting worse, or that severely limit arm movement, warrant a physician visit.
Stiffness after a shoulder injury that makes movement difficult should be evaluated so you get the right exercises early.

faqs.q: Does frozen shoulder go away on its own?
faqs.a: Usually, but slowly and not always completely. The NHS says frozen shoulder can take months or years to get better, though the pain and stiffness will usually go away eventually. The JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline notes that mild to moderate loss of motion and pain may still be present 12 to 18 months in. Therapy aims to ease pain and recover usable motion during that time.

faqs.q: Should I push through pain when stretching a frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: Generally, no. The JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline recommends matching stretching intensity to how irritable the shoulder is, which means gentler stretching when pain is high and firmer stretching as it settles. The NHS also advises against creating your own strenuous exercise routine. Mild discomfort during a stretch is common, but sharp or lingering pain afterward suggests the stretch was too much.

faqs.q: Is frozen shoulder linked to diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes, diabetes is a well-recognized risk factor. The JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline cites a study in which about 38% of men and 24% of women with frozen shoulder had diabetes, compared with about 7% and 5% of similar-age adults. Thyroid disease is also associated with a higher risk.

faqs.q: What are the stages of frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes three stages. In the freezing stage, pain increases and motion is lost over 6 weeks to 9 months. In the frozen stage, pain may ease but stiffness remains for 4 to 6 months. In the thawing stage, motion gradually returns over 6 months to 2 years. Mayo Clinic gives slightly different ranges for each stage.

faqs.q: Can you get frozen shoulder in both shoulders?
faqs.a: You can. The JOSPT adhesive capsulitis guideline reports that having frozen shoulder on one side carries a 5% to 34% risk of the other shoulder being affected in the future, and that both shoulders are affected at the same time in up to 14% of cases. If one shoulder has already been affected, it is worth mentioning early stiffness in the other to your physician.

Not always, but some cases may be. Mayo Clinic notes that one of the most common causes is immobility during recovery from a shoulder injury, broken arm or stroke, and that range-of-motion exercises during that recovery can help prevent it. If your arm is in a sling or you are avoiding using it, ask your physician or therapist which movements are safe to keep doing.
